articles.title: How a hot mic at the WTA Finals caught Jessica Pegula calling Mirra Andreeva a ‘diva’
articles.summary: The WTA Tour has acknowledged that it failed to inform players and their teams at its season-ending, flagship event that practice-court conversations which t...
articles.body:
The WTA Tour has acknowledged that it failed to inform players and their teams at its season-ending, flagship event that practice-court conversations which they believed to be private were being recorded by microphones.

In a statement issued Thursday, the tour said that it "takes full responsibility for failing to inform our players and their teams that microphones, in place to give fans a livestream of the players' practice, were active on the courts" at the WTA Finals , the championship for the best eight singles players and doubles teams of the year.

It followed world No. 5 Jessica Pegula and one of her coaches being caught on a hot mic having a conversation in which Pegula labeled French Open champion Mirra Andreeva a "diva" and said that she had "lost respect" for Andreeva's coach for enabling on-court behavior.

"We sincerely apologize for failing to meet our responsibility to ensure players and coaches were properly informed," the tour said.

Andreeva and Pegula's camps have been contacted for comment.

A private conversation between Pegula and one of her coaches, Mark Knowles, was caught by a microphone on a practice court at Indian Wells Tennis Garden in California. The session was being livestreamed on the WTA Tour's YouTube channel. All the practice streams from this year's event have since been removed from the platform.

The conversation came after a session in which Andreeva won four consecutive games against Pegula, but still, Pegula said, got annoyed enough to hit balls toward Conchita Martínez, the coach with whom the Russian has enjoyed a rapid rise into tennis' upper echelons punctuated by on-court outbursts.

During the conversation, Pegula, 32, said that she had "lost a little respect" for 1994 Wimbledon champion Martínez, because, Pegula said, Martínez "pokes (Andreeva) and eggs on her behavior."

"I think she's a nice girl, she's just a diva. She needs to be humbled," Pegula said of the 19-year-old French Open champion.

Pegula also praised Andreeva, going as far as to suggest that the Russian would surpass Pegula's compatriot and former doubles partner, Coco Gauff, for tennis talent if she could adapt the 22-year-old two-time Grand Slam champion's mentality.

"It's so funny how you see her and then you see Coco's mentality. If she had Coco's mentality, she'd be better than her," Pegula said.

"The serve, everything, all-around, and she moves just as good. But like mentally, she's…" Pegula said.

Pegula, who has become a fixture of the top 10 and more recently the top five in the WTA rankings, reached her debut Grand Slam final at the 2024 U.S. Open, losing to world No. 2 Aryna Sabalenka.

This is not the first incident in 2026 to spark a debate about how much tennis players are filmed and where tournaments place cameras, though filming practice sessions is common practice.

After a 6-1, 6-2 quarterfinal loss to Elina Svitolina at January's Australian Open, Gauff called for "conversations" over which tournament areas have cameras. The American had smashed her racket in frustration in a part of Melbourne Park that she believed to be private , only to see the smash broadcast to the world.

"I kind of have a thing with the broadcast. I feel like certain moments don't need to broadcast," she said.

In a news conference the next day, six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Świątek echoed Gauff's concerns . "The question is, are we tennis players, or are we, like, animals in the zoo where they are observed even when they poop?" Świątek said.

"OK, that was exaggerating obviously, but it would be nice to have some privacy. It would be nice also to, I don't know, have your own process and not always be observed."

A Tennis Australia spokesperson said that "striking the right balance between showcasing the personalities and skills of the players, while ensuring their comfort and privacy is a priority for the AO".

The other three Grand Slams responded to the players' concerns , pledging to either introduce footage reviews before broadcast or to consult players over which areas will and will not have cameras.

The WTA Finals starts Nov. 8, with Gauff and Pegula in the same group; they will play each other on the opening day. Pegula and Andreeva can only meet if they both reach the semifinal stage.

articles.title: WTA Finals: Mirra Andreeva criticised by Jessica Pegula during an interaction with her coach ahead of season-ending tournament
articles.summary: WTA Tour takes "full responsibility" after Mirra Andreeva was labelled a "diva" by American Jessica Pegula ahead of the WTA Finals at Indian Wells; you can watch the ATP Paris Masters live on Sky Sports this week with the WTA Finals in Indian Wells starting on Sunday
articles.body:
American star Pegula is at the centre of controversy after being picked up on a hot mic criticising 19-year-old French Open champion Andreeva and her coach Conchita Martinez at the year-end tournament in California.

The practice session at Indian Wells was live streamed by the Women's Tennis Association on its YouTube channel with the WTA Tour Finals starting on Sunday.

All the practice streams from this year's event have since been removed from the platform.

"Conchita's always been very nice to me, but I lost a little respect for her, because I'm just like, this girl, she's a nice girl. She's a diva. She needs to be humbled. Conchita eggs on her behaviour," the American was heard saying about her rival to one of her coaches, Mark Knowles.

"If I were her coach and my player had just played four great games, she's up 4-0, she gets mad at me and chases me down... I'd tell her not to talk to me like that.

"She's bad... I feel like she needs to be provoked to get fired up and react."

Spaniard Martinez, the 1994 Wimbledon champion, began working with Andreeva in 2024.

Andreeva reached the Wimbledon quarter-finals last year before sealing her first Grand Slam title at Roland Garros in June.

Pegula, who is a member of the WTA players' council, went on to claim that, were Andreeva to adopt Coco Gauff's mentality, she would become a much better player:

"It's so funny 'cause if you see her and Coco's mentality, if she had Coco's mentality, she's better than her. Serve and everything and moves just as good," she said.

But Pegula, runner-up at the 2024 US Open, also praised Andreeva, saying the world No 3 is "wonderful" and "smart".

In a statement issued on Thursday, the WTA Tour said it takes "full responsibility for failing to inform our players and their teams that microphones, in place to give fans a livestream of the players' practice, were active on the courts. We sincerely apologise for failing to meet our responsibility to ensure players and coaches were properly informed".

The WTA went on to explain: "The microphones were intended to capture the ambient sounds of tennis, not player or coach conversations. However, conversations were captured, and we recognise that we failed to ensure the appropriate safeguards were in place.

"We are continuing with live streaming of practice but there will not be any audio."

Pegula has been drawn to face Gauff, world No 1 and defending WTA Finals champion Elena Rybakina, and Linda Noskova, who won her maiden Grand Slam singles title at Wimbledon this year.

Andreeva will avoid Pegula having been drawn alongside Aryna Sabalenka, Elina Svitolina and Karolina Muchova.

The WTA Finals is set to take place between November 8-15 at Indian Wells, before it moves to its new, permanent location of Charlotte, North Carolina in 2027.

The tournament had been hosted in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia for the past two seasons, with Gauff and Rybakina lifting the title in 2024 and 2025 respectively.

articles.title: WTA Apologizes to Jess Pegula for Hot Mic Video, 'Failing to Inform' Players of Live Stream
articles.summary: The WTA apologized Thursday for placing live microphones on the practice court at the WTA Finals this week, unbeknownst to the players.
articles.body:
The WTA apologized Thursday for placing live microphones on the practice court at the WTA Finals this week, unbeknownst to the players.

"The WTA takes full responsibility for failing to inform our players and their teams that microphones, in place to give fans a live stream of the players' practice, were active on the courts at the WTA Finals," the WTA said in a statement . "We sincerely apologize for failing to meet our responsibility to ensure players and coaches feel properly informed."

A portion of the video from the live streamed practice went viral Wednesday due to comments Jessica Pegula made about Mirra Andreeva.

According to BBC Sport's Ben Collins , Pegula was heard calling Andreeva a "diva," and telling her coach that Andreeva "needs to be humbled."

Per Collins, Pegula's agent, Chris McCormack, said Pegula was "completely unaware" of the presence of microphones or that the practice was being live-streamed.

McCormack added that Pegula "has since been in direct contact with those involved, which she felt was important to do personally rather than through the media."

In addition to her critiques of Andreeva, Pegula also praised her ability as a player during the live-streamed practice, saying, "She moves like a cat. She's wonderful. She's got the perfect serve. She's smart. She anticipates well."

Pegula, 32, is the No. 5-ranked player in women's tennis. Although she has won 11 career WTA singles tournaments, Pegula is still in search of her first Grand Slam title.

A loss in the 2024 U.S. Open final is the closest the daughter of Buffalo Bills and Sabres owners Terry and Kim Pegula has come to a Grand Slam championship thus far.

The 19-year-old Andreeva is ranked No. 3 in the world, and she won her first career Grand Slam title earlier this year at the French Open.

Pegula and Andreeva have never faced each other in singles competition, although that could potentially come to an end at the 2026 WTA Finals being held at Indian Wells in California.

While Pegula and Andreeva are in different groups, there is a chance they could meet in the semifinals or finals if both of them advance.

Pegula will begin play at the WTA Finals on Sunday against fellow American Coco Gauff, while Andreeva will take on Elina Svitolina on Monday.

articles.title: Jodie Burrage 'doesn't fear for safety' over online abuse 'because I get so much'
articles.summary: Britain's Jodie Burrage speaks to BBC Sport about the online abuse she received after her recent defeat - and why it no longer comes as a surprise.
articles.body:
After struggling with her blood pressure as she lost her first WTA Tour singles match for 16 months, Jodie Burrage checked in with three things: a doctor, a physiotherapist, and her phone.

On her social media feed there were already messages promising punishment - and others making threats on her life - for losing 3-6 6-3 7-5 to Indian wildcard Vaishnavi Adkar.

"I try not to actually read what they say," Burrage told BBC Sport from Chennai, where she is still competing in the doubles.

"Because we are so used to it - which is really quite sad - I don't fear for my safety.

"You've got to have thick skin. There was some brutal stuff that was said, but I don't take it to heart.

"Sometimes it hurts more than others. If you've already got other stuff going on, or you're not in a great place, and that is put on top of everything else - this tour is tricky enough as it is."

Burrage, who says her blood pressure "tanked" towards the end of the match, decided to share screenshots of the abuse on Instagram to raise awareness of an everyday problem for professional players.

"It happens every match - whether it's win or lose," the 27-year-old Briton said.

"Playing in Wrexham [on the World Tennis Tour last month], I won three matches [and] lost one. But after every single match there was some sort of abuse.

"I think that's where tennis players get it pretty hard - because in tennis you can bet on so many things."

Abuse of players, particularly by angry gamblers, is not a new problem.

Burrage's compatriot Katie Boulter shared with the BBC last year the abuse and death threats she received on a near-daily basis.

This year's WTA and World Tennis report into online abuse, which was based on data from the Signify Group's Threat Matrix service, said "angry gamblers" were responsible for 42% of all verified abuse detected during the 2025 season.

It is why there is so much disquiet about the sponsorship deals some tournaments have struck with gambling firms.

The Davis Cup, for example, has an official sports betting partner, while in August self-described "prediction-market platform" Kalshi signed a multi-year deal with the US Open.

Burrage believes social media platforms "should do more to help".

"I think an ID should be put on every Instagram account, and then that way it makes more people more accountable for their actions on that platform," she said.

"I think it would limit what people would say. People should be accountable for what they say and that's where I think there could be more of a push to change.

All WTA and World Tennis players have access to Threat Matrix's services, which monitor all social media posts directed at players.

The first aim is to provide a rapid assessment of whether an individual's safety is under threat. They can then alert the platforms, and potentially law enforcement agencies, to the offending content.

Names can also be shared with gaming companies, so they have the option of banning offenders from their platforms.

The service can extend to direct messages and even the moderation of accounts, so players never see the message in the first place. But this is not foolproof - and players may feel they would rather know about any threats made against them.

Burrage has recently been able to improve her singles ranking to 474, from a low of 888 in July. Injury prevented her playing singles for nine months and when she returned for the grass court season, sickness held her back.

But she will not allow the abuse to throw her off course.

"I'm at a place where it's all bigger picture for me and everything I'm doing now is to have a good season in 2027," she added.

"I'm building a team that is really good around me. They know where I've been, what I've gone through.

"It's not what you want, but if I have to go through it, then I will."

articles.title: 2026 WTA Finals off to a shaky start with hot mic, individual portraits
articles.summary: WTA Finals drama is off-the-charts in 2026
articles.body:
Tennis fans who thought a US-based WTA Finals would be well run may have a different opinion. Jessica Pegula was caught on a hot mic on an Indian Wells practice court Wednesday. Her conversation with Coach Mark Knowles, centered on Mirra Andreeva who reportedly left their joint practice early. Calling her a "diva" and expressing disappointment in her coach Conchita Martinez for enabling the behavior were not things anyone was supposed to hear.

Pegula did not know there were microphones by the court, an admission WTA made promptly on Thursday. "The WTA takes full responsibility for failing to inform our players and their teams that microphones, in place to give fans a livestream of the players' practice, were active on the courts at the WTA Finals. We sincerely apologize for failing to meet our responsibility to ensure players and coaches were properly informed."

If the hot mic issue was strike one, then the lack of a group photo is strike two. One of the best pre-tournament rituals of the entire tennis season happens at the WTA Finals. The top eight players, dressed to the nines, pose together in an elegant shot.

The WTA Finals is not doing the group photo this year. Instead, there will be eight individual pictures.

Elina Svitolina may be a factor because the Ukrainian does not like to associate with Belarusian and Russian players due to the ongoing Ukrainian war. That would make a small group photo with Aryna Sabalenka and Mirra Andreeva difficult.

For better or worse, the 2026 WTA Finals are turning into a California-based soap opera.
